thread_analysis.thread_summary: An internal [COMPANY] report-review exchange for [COMPANY]'s UXC10 RF test report covers three threads: correcting draft report fields (Company Address, Power Class, Test Voltage) to match the actual Test Plan and test log before approval; explaining why the RF tester's logged Enhanced Power Control setting didn't match the Test Plan's ICS, which traces to a deliberate practice of testing with the ICS set to 'all supported' when the customer's actual declared ICS isn't confidently known, so every possible item gets exercised without affecting other items' results; and clarifying how to log and report a case where an ICS-declared-supported feature is actually unsupported by the DUT, including a historical example involving Enhanced Power Control and a chipset vendor.
all_questions_found: Do the Company Address, Power Class, and Test Voltage fields in the draft RF report match the actual Test Plan and test log, and do they need correcting before approval?
Does a mismatch between the tester's logged Enhanced Power Control setting (True) and the Test Plan ICS's stated value (No) affect the test result or require a retest?
Why would the tester be configured with an ICS setting that differs from the customer's officially declared ICS, and is that an acceptable practice?
If an ICS declares a feature as supported (Yes) but the DUT is actually non-supporting, does that produce a Fail or an Inconclusive result?

If the log confirms the DUT does not respond to a feature it was declared to support, can the product simply be treated as not supporting that feature, or might the feature be incompletely implemented by design rather than genuinely unsupported?

Does a certification testing report need to determine whether a DUT's non-support of a declared feature is due to deliberate design (e.g., the feature being disabled in an initialization routine) versus incomplete implementation, or can it report based on the DUT's factual test response alone?
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The thread covers a report-QA practice of cross-checking draft report fields against the actual Test Plan and log before approval, a deliberate testing practice of configuring the RF tester's ICS to 'all supported' when the customer's actual declared ICS isn't confidently known (so every possible item is exercised, with DUT non-support on any given item not affecting other items' results), and the log-level distinction between Fail and Inconclusive when a DUT's actual behavior contradicts its ICS-declared support for a feature -- illustrated with a historical example where a chipset vendor confirmed SoC-level support for Enhanced Power Control, but the product's own initialization routine disabled the feature, which the lab and customer jointly confirmed and accepted as the basis for a 'non-support' result.
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: Report fields (address, Power Class, Test Voltage, etc.) must reflect the actual values used in the test setup and logged, not assumptions or stale defaults, before a report is approved. Testing with a deliberately broader ('all supported') ICS than the customer's officially confirmed one is an acceptable practice for ensuring complete coverage when the customer's actual ICS isn't confidently known, since items the DUT does not support are recorded as such without contaminating other items' results. When a DUT's actual response contradicts its ICS-declared support for a feature, the log records this as Inconclusive (not Fail), and for certification testing purposes the lab can report based on the DUT's factual test response without needing to determine whether the non-support stems from deliberate design (e.g., a feature disabled in firmware) or incomplete implementation -- that deeper root-cause analysis belongs to a design-verification service, not certification testing.
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: Approving a report with fields that don't match the actual test setup (address, Power Class, Test Voltage) would produce an inaccurate certification record. Treating an ICS-vs-tester-setting mismatch as automatically requiring a retest, without first checking whether it actually affects other test items' results, could trigger unnecessary retesting under a tight schedule. Conversely, assuming a non-support result must always be investigated to the design-verification level before it can be reported would block certification testing reports on questions that are out of scope for that service.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: Before approving a draft test report, verify its key fields against the actual Test Plan and test log rather than assuming defaults are correct. When a tester's logged feature setting disagrees with the Test Plan's ICS, check whether that specific item's outcome is Inconclusive (not Fail) and whether it affects only that item; testing with a deliberately permissive ICS to ensure full coverage, when the customer's actual ICS isn't confidently known, is an acceptable practice as long as non-supported items are correctly recorded. For certification testing (as distinct from a design-verification service), it is acceptable to report a DUT's factual non-support response without resolving whether the underlying cause is a deliberate design choice or an incomplete implementation.
